audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: the Boas 1917 pp. 11-12 passage and both Crippen draft passages are verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated locators. (2) The classification rested on a 1917 grammar plus a modern verb-structure primer; the modern authorities on Tlingit prosody are Leer 1991 (dissertation) and Leer 2001 (tone paper), with Story 1966 (SIL) and Maddieson et al. 2001 (instrumental). I downloaded Leer 1991, Leer 2001, Story 1966 and Crippen's 2013 seminar notes from open archives (ANLA, tlingitlanguage.com), scanned the untexted PDFs, and read the relevant pages. All agree with the classification: Northern/Two-tone and Sanya-Henya Tlingit have lexical tone (2-way and 3-way), Tongass had phonation 'stigmata' instead; no source states a positional word-stress rule; Crippen 2013 says outright that stress 'is poorly documented.. metrical phonology is wide open'. sources.citation: Crippen, James A. 2013. Tlingitology Seminar Notes: Background and Morphology (UBC seminar 1-11 May 2012, summary dated 22 January 2013). 112 pp. PDF from tlingitlanguage.com.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 11: 'there is stress in all dialects, but it is poorly documented and so needs serious phonological research - Leer (1991, 2001) attributes the development of tone as partly due to stress ... metrical phonology is wide open'. p. 10 (Southern): 'stressed long low vowels are typically more low: aandaa [ʔàːnˈtȁː]'. Then 'Tonology (Northern Tlingit dialect): Northern Tlingit has high and low tones', compounding neutralizes H to L except on the last root, CV suffix tone alternation. Confirms: lexical tone is the described system; no stress rule exists in the literature by the field's own account
sources.locator: section 3 'Segmental and tonal phonology', PDF pp. 10-11
